sentences.text: Britain's new PM won under 25,000 votes.
How? Whose seat? And why now?
Britons never vote for a PM. They elect MPs. The biggest party's leader gets the job.
Swap the leader, swap the PM. Seven in ten years.
But here's the weird part: Labour's leader needs a seat in Parliament. He had none.
He was Manchester's mayor, and his party blocked his first try.
Labour lost it. To the Greens.
Then Labour crashed in May's elections. Nearly 100 MPs told Starmer to go.
Now it gets strange: an MP quit, to hand him his seat.
Makerfield voted: one cross, one name. He won by 9,000.
Candidates need a fifth of Labour's MPs. Burnham got 90%. Rivals: zero.
On 20 July, the King made him PM.
Send this to someone who thinks Britain voted for him.
And the crown tag? MPs can't quit. So that MP took a do-nothing Crown job.
Should a new PM face voters first?
